name: Bayesian Ridge Regression
analogy: Think of it as a weighted checklist written by a cautious analyst who says how sure they are. Every feature gets a weight, weights are held close to zero unless the data insists, and the forecast comes with a range instead of a single number.

steps.title: Start with a weighted sum of features
steps.description: Like ordinary linear regression, the forecast is each feature multiplied by a weight and added up. The difference is that each weight is treated as a range of plausible values, not one fixed number.
steps.inExample: The 6-bar-ahead move in MNQ is forecast from 35 base features, each with its own weight, and every weight begins as a wide guess centred on zero.

steps.title: Hold the weights near zero at the start
steps.description: Before seeing data, the model assumes most weights are small. This is the gentle brake that stops it from chasing noise, the same idea as ridge regression but expressed as a belief about the weights.
steps.inExample: No feature is allowed to look important until the training bars give evidence for it.

steps.title: Update the beliefs with the training bars
steps.description: Looking at the bars and their outcomes, the model narrows each weight's range. Features that help repeatedly get a weight clearly away from zero; features that do not stay near zero with a wide range.
steps.inExample: After 40,000 bars, the weight on the 6-bar return settles slightly negative, while most volume-based weights stay near zero.

steps.title: Learn how noisy the target is
steps.description: The model also estimates how much of the outcome is unexplained noise and how strong the brake on the weights should be. Both are learned from the data in a few rounds of adjustment, so there is no strength setting to tune by hand.
steps.inExample: It concludes the typical 6-bar move not explained by the features is about 48 points, which is most of the movement.

steps.title: Forecast with a range
steps.description: For a new bar it computes the average forecast using the typical weights. It then widens the forecast into a range by combining the unexplained noise with the leftover uncertainty about the weights.
steps.inExample: For the 14:35 bar the average forecast is a rise of 5 points, with a spread of 48 points around it.

useFor.task: A forecast that states its own uncertainty
useFor.example: Predicting the 30-minute MNQ move together with a range, so position size can shrink when the range is wide.

useFor.task: Noisy targets with many correlated features
useFor.example: Fitting a forward-return target from many overlapping momentum indicators without hand-tuning a penalty.
Setting a floor for walk-forward folds before trying trees or neural networks.

useFor.task: Seeing which features the data really supports
useFor.example: Reading which weights are clearly away from zero and which stay uncertain, as an honest check on a favourite indicator.

avoidWhen: The relationship is clearly curved or depends on combinations of features; a straight weighted sum cannot represent it and a tree or network is better.
The target has very fat tails, as price moves often do; the model assumes bell-shaped noise, so its ranges will be too narrow in the tails.

example.scenario: A 5-minute MNQ bar closes at 14:35. The model forecasts the change in the close 6 bars (30 minutes) later, in points, along with how uncertain that forecast is.

input.summary: One row of features for the bar that just closed, rescaled the way the training bars were.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 14:35 five-minute bar closed.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; under 30 is commonly read as oversold.

fields.name: return over the last 6 bars
fields.value: down about a third of a percent
fields.meaning: How much price has fallen over the previous 30 minutes.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar, a measure of how much the market is moving.

fields.name: distance from the 50-bar moving average
fields.meaning: How far the close sits below its recent average price.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading in this bar was compared with the recent norm.

output.summary: An average forecast for the 30-minute move and the spread around it.

fields.name: forecast change in the close after 6 bars
fields.meaning: The model's average expectation of how far the close will be above this bar's close.

fields.name: uncertainty of the forecast
fields.meaning: One standard spread around the forecast, combining market noise and doubt about the weights.

fields.name: range holding about 90 percent of outcomes
fields.meaning: The forecast plus and minus about 80 points, where the model expects the move to land nine times in ten.

fields.name: forecast in US dollars per contract
fields.meaning: 5 points times 2 US dollars per MNQ point, before any trading costs.

example.reading: The forecast of 5 points is tiny next to a 48-point spread, which is what to expect from a noisy market. Use the spread as much as the forecast: it says how large a position the call can carry, and a forecast this small has to clear commission and slippage before it is worth acting on.
